title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how K-12 learning should be designed when AI is introduced as a collaborative partner rather than only as a tool. The authors argue that existing AIED work has emphasized learning with AI or learning about AI, but less attention has been given to the quality of student-AI collaboration and the surrounding learning environment needed to support it.

The study is based on semi-structured, in-depth interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers in AI in education, drawn from primary and secondary schools participating in software leading schools, AI pilot schools, and AI convergence high schools. Using a thematic analysis informed by a student-AI collaboration framework, the authors examine views on curriculum, student-AI interaction, environment, and how collaboration evolves over time.

Teachers emphasized that SAC should build students' capacity, subject knowledge, and cross-disciplinary problem solving through authentic and creative tasks. They also argued for process-oriented assessment, explicit instruction in AI principles, data literacy, error analysis, AI ethics, and AI experiences in daily life, plus AI systems that provide scaffolding, intuitive interfaces, and varied digital tools. At the system level, the paper concludes that effective student-AI collaboration requires flexible classrooms, strong digital infrastructure, teacher professional learning, systematic policy support, collaborative school culture, and a safe-to-fail environment that treats errors as part of learning.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative interview study with 10 teachers using thematic analysis. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically coherent for eliciting practitioner perspectives, but it does not provide experimental or quasi-experimental evidence on intervention effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no measured student outcomes or effect sizes, so there is no demonstrated impact to score. Its value is in design guidance and identifying likely implementation needs, but actual educational impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: teacher perspectives on student-AI collaboration for K-12 learning design, including AI as a collaborative learning partner, scaffolding agent, and learning mate

finding.finding_summary: In interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers in AIED, participants emphasized that successful student-AI collaboration requires coordinated systemic supports: a nationwide AIED policy, cross-sector governance, flexible school structures, teacher professional development, and collaborative school culture. This is a qualitative perception study with no effect size reported; findings point to strong perceived institutional importance rather than measured impact.
finding.measure: teacher interview themes on policy, governance, school structure, and professional capacity building

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified capacity building, subject-matter knowledge building, interdisciplinary learning, authentic problem solving, creative tasks, and collaboration performance as core goals of student-AI collaboration. The paper reports qualitative consensus across 10 teachers rather than quantitative outcomes; no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: teacher interview themes on higher-order thinking, collaboration, creativity, and problem solving goals

finding.finding_summary: Teachers argued that student-AI collaboration should support motivation, persistence, confidence, and a 'safe to fail' mindset, and that AI should be designed to encourage students when they struggle. These are qualitative perceptions from 10 teachers; no quantitative effect size or confidence interval was reported.
finding.measure: teacher interview themes on motivation, persistence, engagement, and affective support

finding.finding_summary: Teachers viewed AI systems as potentially reducing repetitive work by automating parts of data collection, personalized support, and workflow integration with existing school platforms. However, the paper does not measure workload reduction empirically; it reports anticipated efficiency benefits and cautions that poor integration could add work for teachers.
finding.measure: teacher perceptions of workload, automation, and platform integration
